claims.text: High-entropy alloys are inherently chemically homogeneous and single-phase.
A homogeneous single-phase HEA microstructure promotes rapid formation of a continuous protective passive oxide or tribolayer.
The protective surface layer continuously regenerates after mechanical damage.
The regenerated surface layer reduces both mechanical abrasion and localized electrochemical attack.
Equiatomic or optimized AlCoCrFeNi is an example of a suitable homogeneous single-phase HEA.
At moderate wear and corrosion levels, oxide regeneration can remain kinetically viable.
The passive layer's stability and self-healing capability are mediated by chemical uniformity and possible short-range order in the HEA.
High configurational entropy suppresses phase segregation.
High configurational entropy minimizes localized galvanic cells.
A surface exposed by wear is rapidly reoxidized into a protective layer.
The self-replenishing layer limits oxygen and ion ingress.
The HEA will have a lower combined wear-corrosion degradation rate than a matched lower-complexity alloy.
The HEA will lose less material through wear than the baseline.
The HEA will exhibit less corrosion penetration than the baseline.
The HEA's combined degradation will be less than the sum of the individual wear and corrosion processes observed in the baseline.
A lower-configurational-entropy baseline will not form as robust or rapidly regenerating a passive layer under identical conditions.
The predicted advantage should hold when the medium does not destabilize the oxide and wear proceeds more slowly than repassivation.
The predicted advantage may fail when wear or oxide dissolution outpaces regeneration of the protective layer.
Wear rate, corrosion penetration, passive-layer properties, and repassivation kinetics can be compared between the HEA and a matched conventional-alloy control.
Failure to observe lower combined degradation or a more robust, self-healing passive layer in the HEA would falsify the hypothesis.
